nameStory: The tiger sorubim gets its fierce name from the distinctive dark stripes that run along its silvery body, resembling a tiger's bold markings. 'Sorubim' comes from the indigenous South American name for these impressive catfish, while 'tiger' perfectly captures those eye-catching bands that make this fish unmistakable.
description: The tiger sorubim is a massive South American catfish that's native to the Amazon Basin but has been spotted once in New England waters. This impressive fish can grow up to 51 inches long, making it one of the largest catfishes you might encounter. Its most striking feature is the pattern of dark vertical bands across a silvery-gray body, combined with long whiskers that give it an almost prehistoric appearance.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bold black or dark brown vertical bands stripe across a silvery-gray body, creating an unmistakable tiger-like pattern that remains vivid even when the fish is stressed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, torpedo-shaped body that feels surprisingly firm and muscular to the touch, with a slightly flattened head that tapers to a pointed snout

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large terminal mouth positioned at the front of the head with a slightly protruding lower jaw, surrounded by prominent barbels that feel smooth and flexible

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Large, fan-like pectoral fins with sharp spines that can lock into position, and a distinctive adipose fin (small fleshy fin behind the dorsal fin) typical of catfish

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Exceptionally large for New England waters, potentially reaching over 4 feet in length with a hefty, substantial body weight that requires two hands to lift safely

habitat: Tiger sorubim are not native to New England and the single observation likely represents an escaped or released aquarium fish. If encountered, it would most likely be found in warmer river systems or large lakes during summer months. These fish prefer deeper waters with moderate current and are typically found near the bottom where they hunt for prey.

seasonality.spring: Any tiger sorubim in New England waters would be sluggish in cool spring temperatures, likely seeking the warmest available water near shorelines or shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active period if present, when warm water temperatures allow normal feeding and movement behavior in deeper river channels or lake areas.
seasonality.fall: Activity would decrease significantly as water temperatures drop, with the fish seeking deeper, more stable thermal areas if it survived the season.
seasonality.winter: Extremely unlikely to survive New England winter temperatures, as this tropical species requires much warmer water than our region provides.

funFact: In their native Amazon waters, tiger sorubim are known to migrate incredible distances - sometimes over 1,000 miles upstream to spawn, making them one of the longest-distance migrating fish in the world!
confusionNotes: The distinctive tiger stripes make this fish nearly impossible to confuse with any native New England species. The closest might be a very large channel catfish, but channel cats lack the bold vertical banding and have a more rounded, less torpedo-shaped body.
contextualKnowledge: This is an exotic species that should not be in New England waters naturally. If you encounter one, it's likely an escaped or illegally released aquarium fish. Tiger sorubim are popular in the aquarium trade when small, but grow far too large for home tanks, leading to unfortunate releases into local waterways.
compareHints: As the only Pseudoplatystoma species recorded in New England, compare it to other large catfish in the long-whiskered catfish family. Unlike our native channel catfish, tiger sorubim have much more pronounced vertical banding, a more streamlined body shape, and can reach significantly larger sizes. The barbels are also typically longer and more prominent than those of native catfish species.
